rationale: The hypothesis posits that progressive or postnatal microcephaly (HP:0005484) and severe axial hypotonia (HP:0008936) occur in over 60-80% of individuals with RNU2-2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE 119, OMIM #621304). The available literature confirms that generalized/axial hypotonia is highly prevalent in biallelic RNU2-2 DEE cohorts (specifically documented in 11 of 14 [79%] patients by Henry et al., 2026), and microcephaly is frequently observed (Jackson et al., 2026; Samanta, 2026). However, the literature reveals key conflicts: (1) Jackson et al. (2026) emphasize that the recessive RNU2-2 syndrome is clinically, genetically, and mechanistically distinct from the dominant RNU2-2 disorder, whereas OMIM #621304 specifically designates autosomal dominant DEE 119; and (2) quantitative prevalence demonstrating that postnatal/progressive microcephaly specifically exceeds 60-80% is not reported in the available cohort datasets.

evidence.text: In a deep-phenotyping cohort of 14 individuals with biallelic RNU2-2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, hypotonia was present in 11 of 14 (79%) individuals, alongside hypertonia in 11 of 14 (79%) and progressive orofacial hypotonia.

source.quote: Hypotonia and hypertonia were present in 11 of 14 (79%) and 11 of 14 (79%) individuals, … fissures, and features consistent with progressive orofacial hypotonia were observed.

evidence.text: Biallelic RNU2-2 syndrome is clinically delineated as a severe DEE presenting with generalized hypotonia, microcephaly, abnormal central motor function, and intellectual disability, but is clinically and mechanistically distinct from dominant RNU2-2 disorder.

source.title: Biallelic variants in RNU2-2 cause a remarkably frequent developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
source.quote: We show that the recessive RNU2-2 syndrome is genetically, clinically and mechanistically distinct from the dominant RNU2-2 disorder.

evidence.text: RNU2-2 variants cause both dominant and recessive NDDs; dominant and recessive forms share overlapping features with frequent epilepsy, but quantitative microcephaly penetrance exceeding 60-80% is not established across all cohorts.

source.title: Systematic analysis of snRNA genes reveals frequent RNU2-2 variants in dominant and recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
source.quote: Dominant and recessive RNU2-2 NDDs share overlapping clinical features, with frequent epilepsy.

evidence.text: A clinical report of biallelic RNU2-2 neurodevelopmental disorder presenting with severe DEE and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome documented persistent truncal hypotonia, appendicular hyperreflexia, and microcephaly (<3rd percentile).

source.title: Biallelic RNU2-2–related neurodevelopmental disorder presenting as Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
source.quote: a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy(DEE) … with persistent truncal hypotonia, appendicular hyperreflexia … and clorazepate), and microcephaly (51 cm, <3rd percentile).

conflicts: OMIM #621304 is classified as autosomal dominant developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 119, whereas the quantitative 79% hypotonia frequency is specifically derived from individuals with biallelic (recessive) RNU2-2 variants.

Jackson et al. (2026) state that recessive RNU2-2 syndrome is clinically distinct from the dominant disorder, preventing direct extrapolation of phenotypic frequencies between dominant DEE 119 and recessive RNU2-2 cohorts.

While microcephaly is frequently noted as a comorbid feature, existing published cohorts do not confirm that progressive or postnatal microcephaly independently achieves the hypothesized 60-80% frequency threshold.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact penetrance of postnatal versus congenital microcephaly in dominant versus biallelic RNU2-2 cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Differentiating head circumference trajectories between dominant DEE 119 and recessive RNU2-2 encephalopathies is critical to establishing whether microcephaly serves as a reliable discriminating biomarker.

new_directions.question_text: How do co-occurring axial hypotonia and appendicular hypertonia differentiate RNU2-2 DEE from other noncoding spliceosomal encephalopathies (such as RNU4-2-related ReNU syndrome)?
new_directions.rationale: Henry et al. observed co-occurring hypotonia (79%) and hypertonia (79%) in biallelic RNU2-2 patients, a mixed motor phenotype that could improve phenotypic specificity relative to clinically overlapping DEEs.
